doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Milt Hinton and black musicians' reticence about race
summary: Fillius says Hinton and others never discuss race, mentions Hinton's childhood memory, and praises him and Mona.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you find the same type of feeling in the other fellas of that era that you got to know like Milt Hinton?

Well I think so but I don’t know him that well. Milt Hinton I’m pretty sure is broad minded about anything. But he is from an era where you don’t display your feelings. And most of the black guys I know, Terry and Sweets Edison and people like that — you just never get on that subject. You know that they like you. You know that you’re their friend and that there’s no color bar between you. But I don’t think you ever get far enough in their innermost thoughts to know what they think. Milt Hinton for example. His first memory when he was three years old he was looking out the window to see his uncle hung by the Ku Klux Klan. You know, that’s got to do something to you. And I always wondered how Milt could be so broad minded and accept whatever came along with that in his head. I’d say it would have to leave a scar. But Milt and Mona have millions of white friends. I mean boy, there’s nothing like it. More so than anybody I think.
Yeah, they attract — people want to be near them.
You know there’s something about them that they make you feel good.
